titre: Risking Your Life for a Useless Necklace
accroche: Crossing the ocean in a fragile canoe to trade an object you can neither eat nor sell.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the Trobriand Islands, off Papua New Guinea, men set out to sea in outrigger canoes, sometimes for several days, at the risk of storms and shipwreck. Their cargo has no practical use: necklaces of red shell (*soulava*) and armbands of white shell (*mwali*), which are not eaten, are almost never worn, and are not sold. This is what the anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski observed during two stays between 1915 and 1918, in the fieldwork that would become *Argonauts of the Western Pacific* (1922). That fieldwork would found the modern method of ethnographic fieldwork: living for months among the people you study, rather than questioning them in passing.

## One ring, two directions of travel

This system has a name, the kula. The *soulava* necklaces circulate from island to island in one direction; the *mwali* armbands circulate in the opposite direction, along the same sea routes, among some twenty communities of the Massim archipelago. A kula partner receives an armband on one side and must give a necklace on the other, and vice versa. Never both at once, never as immediate payment for a service. The object never stays long in the same hands: it moves on, carried by its own reputation, and gains in value the farther and the longer it has circulated.

What Malinowski sought to understand, precisely, is why men would accept such a risk for an object that serves no concrete purpose. His answer: the kula is not a disguised form of commerce. It is a system of alliances in which the exchange of the object seals a relationship of trust that lasts a lifetime, and in which the prestige of briefly owning a famous piece is well worth its use value, which is zero. Trobriand society being matrilineal, a man does not inherit from his father: rank and property pass from the maternal uncle to the nephew, and it is to this uncle that a man pays the fee that gives him entry into the kula.

## What this shifts

The kula long served as a counterexample to the idea that human exchange is originally reduced to utilitarian barter: I give you what you need, you give me what I need. Here, the object exchanged explicitly has no use value. Its only function is to keep a relationship circulating. What the men risk their lives to carry is not a good. It is a bond.

The same logic, more discreetly, can be found whenever a symbolic object changes hands with no other function than to maintain a relationship: the wedding ring that is never resold, the trophy passed along in a club, the medal that has value only because it has circulated. The kula does not describe a Melanesian oddity; it makes visible, in its pure state, a mechanism that market economies usually cover with a utilitarian veneer.

repere.texte: Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922) documents the kula on the basis of fieldwork Malinowski carried out between 1915 and 1918 in the Trobriand Islands: one of the first examples of prolonged immersion in modern ethnography.
repere.source: Bronisław Malinowski, Argonauts of the Western Pacific, 1922

carte.punch: They risk their lives for a necklace that serves no purpose.
carte.idee: In the Trobriand Islands, men cross the ocean in fragile canoes to trade shell necklaces and armbands with no practical use. Malinowski showed that this object does not carry a use value. It carries a relationship.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Concise overview of the exchange system.

quiz.question: Why do kula partners exchange shell necklaces and armbands?
choix: Because these objects have great nutritional value
To seal and maintain a lasting relationship of alliance
To resell them afterward in neighboring markets
Because colonial law required them to
quiz.explication: The soulava and the mwali have no practical use: their exchange seals a relationship of trust between partners, often passed down over several generations, and not a trade in useful or resalable goods.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How do the soulava necklaces and the mwali armbands circulate in relation to each other in the kula system?
choix: Both objects always circulate together, never separately, in the same direction
The necklaces circulate only by day, the armbands only by night
Each object circulates only once before being buried with its last owner
The soulava necklaces circulate in one direction, the mwali armbands in the opposite direction, along the same sea routes
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The kula system sends the soulava necklaces from island to island in one direction, and the mwali armbands in the opposite direction, along the same sea routes, among some twenty communities of the Massim archipelago.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Malinowski's fieldwork in the Trobriand Islands consist of, and what does it establish for ethnography?
choix: A single three-day visit, conducted by mail-in questionnaire to village chiefs
Ten years of observation from a distance in Australia, never setting foot on the islands
Two stays between 1915 and 1918, founding the prolonged-immersion method of modern ethnographic fieldwork
A British military expedition charged with mapping the local sea routes
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Malinowski carries out two stays between 1915 and 1918 in the Trobriand Islands, living for months among the people he studies rather than questioning them in passing, which founds the modern method of ethnographic fieldwork.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What general idea about human exchange does the kula serve as a counterexample to?
choix: The idea that human exchange is originally reduced to utilitarian barter of goods each person needs
The idea that maritime trade appeared later than land trade
The idea that matrilineal societies know no form of organized exchange
The idea that ritual objects never have value outside their religious use
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The kula long served as a counterexample to the idea that human exchange is originally reduced to utilitarian barter (I give you what you need, you give me what I need): here the object exchanged explicitly has no use value.
